lesson_title: The Lawn and the Driveway: Why Rivers Flood
hook_text: Throw a bucket of water on the lawn, then on the driveway. One of them is your whole city.
clip_script: Fill a bucket at the outside tap. Throw it across the lawn — the water darkens the grass and it's gone. Now throw it across the paved driveway — it's at the gate before the bucket is even empty. Same water. Different surface. And that difference explains every flood on the news. The lawn is a healthy catchment: grass catching rain, roots holding the soil open, a wetland at the bottom of the valley storing the surplus. Rain goes in and reaches the river slowly, over days. The driveway is everything that refuses to drink: bare rock, ground baked hard, soil already full from last week's storms — and above all, the city. Tar, paving, rooftops, with stormwater pipes aimed straight at the river. Build a suburb and you've paved your catchment for good. That's why the Jukskei — a stream you can step over in winter — rose in minutes on the third of December 2022 and swept away at least fourteen people near Alexandra. Its catchment is northern Johannesburg: wall-to-wall driveway. So next time a flood makes headlines, ask the geographer's question: was it really just the rain — or did we pave the lawn ourselves?
visual_style: Split screen: a bucket thrown over grass and over paving in slow motion; the grass morphing into green hills with a wetland, the paving morphing into rooftops and tar; a small stream rising fast under storm light.
pacing: Playful experiment up front, the two morphs land the concept, the Jukskei beat lands the stakes, closing question lingers.
